description: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed environments, risking immune changes, bone loss, and behavioral health issues. Cosmo Vitals lets astronauts self-monitor via daily check-ins across 5 key health areas mapped to these hazards, with color-coded alerts, a radar chart, 14-day trends, a clickable body map, weekly reports, and streak gamification — turning risk awareness into a simple, actionable daily habit.
summary: Cosmo Vitals is a crew health terminal for astronauts on long-duration missions. Space radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity change and closed environments change the body slowly, and astronauts must notice these changes in themselves. Our web app turns this into a one-minute daily habit. Each crew member answers ten plain-language questions across five health areas, each mapped to one of NASA's five hazards, and can add vitals, a reaction-time test and a 3D body map. Cosmo Vitals learns each person's own baseline and scores every new reading against it. Alerts open early (WATCH at 1.8 standard deviations, ACT at 3.0), clear with hysteresis, and explain why they fired, what to do and which NASA research applies. Dashboards show a Health Shape radar chart, 14-day trends and a weekly report. A mission console supports five environments, crews of 1 to 8, a what-if simulator, and ground sync that handles contact windows, blackouts and delay. It is a monitoring aid, not a diagnosis, and data stays on the device.
details:
Detailed Project Description

Cosmo Vitals is a daily health check-in for astronauts on long missions, built for the moments when help is far away. It learns each crew member's own normal, warns early when readings drift, and tells the astronaut in plain words why an alert fired and what to do next.

How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

1. Personal Baseline Scoring: Instead of one fixed limit for everyone, every reading is scored against that person's own normal:

  • Baseline – built from seven earlier daily check-ins of each crew member.
  • Check-in rules – each vital (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, weight, glucose, sleep, exercise) is compared with a reference range and with the person's baseline (for example, resting heart rate 10 bpm above baseline raises a WATCH).
  • Mission console score – z = (reading − personal mean) ÷ personal standard deviation, calculated for 12 simulated signals (dose rate, sleep, reaction time, mood, heart rate, HRV, cabin CO₂, SpO₂, temperature, noise, breathing and exercise load).

2. Three-Level Alerts with Hysteresis: WATCH is raised at 1.8σ and ACT at 3.0σ. An alert only clears when the reading falls below 1.2σ, so a value hovering near a line does not switch the alert on and off.

3. Pattern and Combination Findings: Findings are labelled by how long they last:

  • Isolated – one day.
  • Developing – two days in a row.
  • Persistent – three or more days.
  • A persistent WATCH becomes an ALERT after seven days, and a combination of signs can raise a finding that no single reading would.

Every finding says why it fired and what to do next, with NASA evidence. Cosmo Vitals never diagnoses.

4. Blackout-Ready Link Model: Each mission environment (spacecraft, space station, lunar rover, lunar surface base, Mars rover or habitat) has its own link profile with a one-way delay and contact windows (for example 12 minutes and two 2-hour windows a day on the Mars profile). Check-ins are saved on the device, queued during a blackout and synced at the next contact window. A simulated flight-surgeon (Ground) view shows what Earth would see.

WHAT IT DOES

Cosmo Vitals is a daily health check-in for astronauts on long missions, when help is far away. A call to Earth can take about 12 minutes each way on a trip to Mars, and a doctor cannot walk in, so crew members need to notice slow changes in themselves. Each day every crew member answers ten plain-language sliders across five health areas: Sleep & Energy, Mood & Stress, Muscle & Joint Pain, Balance & Dizziness and Symptoms. Each area is tied to one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity change and closed environment. Optional vitals, a reaction-time test and a 3D body map add more signals.

HOW IT WORKS

The app builds a personal baseline for every crew member and scores each new reading in standard deviations from that person's own normal, instead of using one fixed limit for everyone. An alert opens at 1.8 sigma (WATCH) or 3.0 sigma (ACT) and clears below 1.2 sigma, so alerts do not flicker on and off. Findings are classed as single reading, two in a row, persistent pattern or combined signs, with three escalation levels: monitor, contact ground, urgent. Every alert shows why it fired, action steps, and links to NASA Human Research Program evidence. The app never names a disease and never suggests medication. All analysis runs in the browser with no server calls, so the app keeps working if the connection drops after it has loaded. Ground contact is simulated: during a blackout, check-ins and alerts wait in a queue and are sent when the next contact window opens.

FEATURES

Health Shape radar chart, 14-day trends with OK, WATCH and ALERT zones, downloadable weekly report, 3D anatomical body, reminders, streaks and ranks, five mission environments (spacecraft, space station, lunar rover, lunar base, Mars habitat), crews of 1 to 8, a what-if simulator (solar particle event, CO2 scrubber fault, insomnia streak, skipped exercise), and a simulated flight-surgeon view for the ground team.

BENEFITS

Earlier awareness of small changes, clear next steps when ground contact is delayed, and a simple one-minute daily habit that keeps the whole crew engaged.

INTENDED IMPACT

To help crews on future Moon and Mars missions notice health problems while they are still small, and to give the ground team a clear picture even with delay. The same idea could later support other isolated teams on Earth, such as polar stations or ships.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND HARDWARE

TypeScript, TanStack Start, React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Radix UI, three.js for the 3D body, Recharts for charts, Vitest (more than 80 automated tests) and Vite. No special hardware is needed: it runs in any modern web browser on a phone or computer, and all data stays in the user's browser. Sensor streams are simulated and labelled SIM in the app, and real sensors can replace them. Live demo: support.mumair.site

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most health trackers compare you with an average. Cosmo Vitals compares you with yourself, so a normal sleep for one person is not mistaken for a bad night for another. Every alert explains itself in plain words and tells the astronaut what to do, which matters when no doctor is nearby. We turned NASA's five hazards into five simple health areas, added a small game of streaks and ranks (Cadet to Commander) so the check-in actually happens every day, and built a what-if simulator so a crew can see how alerts react to a solar storm or a CO2 fault before it happens.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Safety: a monitoring aid, never a diagnosis. Privacy: no data leaves the device. Accessibility: every status is written as a word, not color alone. Communication: delay, contact windows and blackouts are built in. Honesty: radiation doses are rough planning values, simulated data is clearly marked, the ground link is simulated, and the app is a prototype, not a medical device.

NASA DATA AND RESOURCES

  • NASA Human Research Program hazard pages: Space Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity Fields, and Hostile Closed Environments (nasa.gov/hrp).
  • NASA Human Research Roadmap: humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov
  • NASA NTRS 20160012725: "Relationship Between Carbon Dioxide Levels and Reported Congestion and Headaches on the International Space Station" (used as evidence for the cabin CO2 alert).
  • NASA NTRS 20170005625: "Risk of Cardiac Rhythm Problems During Spaceflight" (used as evidence for heart rate and HRV).
  • NASA reference pages for human research studies, such as Standard Measures, ARCHeR and CIPHER (nasa.gov/reference), linked as context in the app.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)

Claude and ChatGPT -were used for brainstorming, collecting information, and correcting grammar and sentence structure for the final submission. Google was also used for information gathering, and AI tools helped create some parts of the images and videos.
